title: The Sharpe Pint: Ticking Fees, Tariff Walls, and the HFT Liquidity Trap

opening_mood.text: Alright? Grab a pint. If you thought the summer lull was finally here, Donald Trump, a coalition of state attorneys general, and a few high-frequency trading algorithms had other ideas. This week has been a bruising run for risk assets, with big tech taking a pasting, geopolitical tensions spiking Brent crude, and some eye-watering M&A bleed. Let's get you sharp for the week ahead.

content.text: 1. The $110B Paramount-Warner Merger Hits a Massive Red Light

The Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger has officially hit the buffers. Paramount Skydance has agreed to a months-long delay of its $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, pushing the timeline out to as late as June 2027. This comes after a coalition of 12 state attorneys general (led by California and New York) and the Writers Guild of America sued to block the deal on antitrust grounds.

Why it matters: This isn't just a delay; it's a financial bleed. Under the terms of the deal, if it didn't close by September 30, Paramount agreed to pay Warner shareholders a 'ticking fee' of $0.25 per share per day. That translates to an eye-watering $7 million a day, or $650 million a quarter. If the deal falls through entirely, Paramount is on the hook for a $7 billion breakup fee. Talk about a high-stakes waiting game.

The City angle: For the merger arb desks, this is a bloodbath. The spread is widening faster than the Thames at high tide. For investment bankers, it's a stark warning about the dangers of agreeing to aggressive ticking fees in a hostile regulatory environment. It also shows that state AGs are now a major force in antitrust, willing to step in even when the DOJ gives a nod.

items: What to say at work: 'Agreeing to a $7 million-a-day ticking fee while facing a state-led antitrust trial is an absolute shocker. Paramount is essentially bleeding cash while waiting for a judge to decide if they can even buy the thing. It's a massive win for the state AGs and a nightmare for arb desks.'

content.text: 2. Trump Rebuilds the Tariff Wall with Section 301 Forced Labor Levies

Donald Trump has rebuilt his tariff wall, and this time he's using a clever legal backdoor. The US has imposed new tariffs ranging from 10% to 12.5% on imports from 60 economies, including the UK, EU, Japan, and China. Enacted under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, the tariffs ostensibly target countries that fail to effectively ban goods made with forced labour. They replace the temporary Section 122 levies that expired on Friday.

Why it matters: This is a massive macroeconomic shock. The new trade action covers a staggering 99.4% of US imports (excluding USMCA partners like Canada/Mexico, and oil/gas). Countries with no forced labour import bans (like the UK, Japan, China) face 12.5% tariffs, while those with unenforced bans (like the EU) face 10%. It's a universal tariff in all but name.

The City angle: For macro funds and currency traders, this is highly inflationary. It puts upward pressure on US yields and could force the Fed to keep rates higher for longer. It also triggers immediate retaliatory threats from trading partners like Brazil and Australia, raising the spectre of a full-blown global trade war.

items: What to say at work: 'Trump's use of Section 301 forced labour investigations is a clever legal workaround to rebuild his tariff wall after the Supreme Court struck down his previous 'Liberation Day' tariffs. By covering nearly 99% of US imports, this is effectively a universal tariff by another name. The immediate fallout will be inflationary, which complicates the Fed's rate path and puts pressure on global supply chains.'

content.text: 3. Intel's Turnaround Gets an AI Shot in the Arm

Intel's turnaround has finally found some traction, thanks to a surprise boost from the AI boom. The chipmaker reported Q2 revenue of $16.1 billion (up 25% YoY) and forecast Q3 revenue of $15.8B to $16.8B, smashing Wall Street's estimates. Crucially, Intel secured Elon Musk's Tesla as a customer for its next-generation 14A process for the 'Terafab' AI chip project, and raised its 2026 capex forecast to over $20 billion.

Why it matters: Amidst a brutal week for the 'Magnificent Seven' (which saw an $800 billion tech wipeout earlier in the week due to capex fears), Intel provided a rare bright spot. The surge in demand is driven by 'agentic AI' (autonomous AI agents), which has sparked a massive resurgence in demand for data centre CPUs (Intel's bread and butter), rather than just Nvidia's GPUs.

The City angle: This is a major structural shift in the AI trade. For the past two years, the narrative was 'GPUs only, CPUs are dead.' Intel's results show that as AI moves from training to inference and agentic workloads, the CPU is reasserting itself as a core foundation.

items: What to say at work: 'Intel's earnings show that the AI infrastructure trade is broadening out. The shift toward agentic AI is driving a massive resurgence in data centre CPU demand, which caught the industry off guard. Securing Tesla as a foundry customer for their 14A process is a massive validation of Lip-Bu Tan's turnaround strategy.'

content.text: 4. Volkswagen's China Profit Machine Collapses, Forcing a Brutal Restructuring

Volkswagen is facing the deepest crisis in its 89-year history. The German carmaker reported a 9.5% drop in Q2 operating profit to €3.5 billion and slashed its full-year revenue forecast, now expecting sales revenue to decline by up to 3% (reversing a previous forecast of a 3% increase). The culprit is a collapse in its highly profitable China joint ventures, where proportionate operating profit is on track to fall from €958 million in 2025 to as low as €200 million this year.

Why it matters: VW is facing the deepest crisis in its history. CEO Oliver Blume is pushing for a radical restructuring, including up to 100,000 job cuts globally, cutting its model lineup by half, and potentially closing four German factories.

The City angle: This is a classic case of structural disruption. European legacy auto is getting absolutely crushed by cheap, highly competitive Chinese EV manufacturers (like BYD) both in China and increasingly in Europe. For equity analysts, VW's cash flow swing (automotive net cash flow swung to a €3.2 billion inflow) is a temporary band-aid masking a terminal decline in its core profit engine.

items: What to say at work: 'Volkswagen's downgrade is a stark reminder of how quickly a dominant market position can evaporate. China was VW's profit engine for decades, but that joint-venture profit has essentially collapsed due to local EV competition. Blume's plan to cut 100,000 jobs and close German plants shows that legacy auto has no choice but to shrink its way to survival.'

content.text: 5. Alphabet's $98 Billion GAAP Illusion Distorts S&P 500 Earnings

According to FactSet's earnings update on July 24, 2026, the S&P 500 is reporting impressive Q2 earnings growth, but the numbers are heavily distorted by Alphabet. Alphabet reported a massive GAAP EPS surprise ($9.11 vs. $2.88 estimated) which included a one-off gain of $98 billion.

Why it matters: Alphabet's massive gain artificially inflated the entire S&P 500's earnings surprise. In aggregate, S&P 500 companies are reporting earnings 39.3% above estimates. However, if you exclude Alphabet, the aggregate earnings surprise falls to a much more modest 12.6%.

The City angle: This is a vital lesson in 'under-the-hood' analysis for equity research and quant analysts. Relying on headline index-level metrics right now is incredibly dangerous because a single non-operating gain at a megacap tech giant is masking the true operational performance of the broader market.

items: What to say at work: 'The headline S&P 500 earnings surprise of nearly 40% is a complete GAAP illusion. Alphabet's $98 billion one-off gain is doing almost all the heavy lifting. Once you strip that out, the aggregate surprise drops to 12.6%. It's a classic reminder of why you have to look past the index-level aggregates to understand true corporate health.'

content.text: 6. Geopolitics Back with a Vengeance: Brent Crude Touches $101

Oil prices spiked on Friday, with Brent crude touching $101 a barrel early in the day following a 13th round of US air strikes in Iran. While prices retreated slightly later in the session, the escalation in the Middle East continues to put severe strain on global energy supplies and keeps inflation worries front and centre for central bankers.

Why it matters: Just as markets were hoping for a summer lull, the widening conflict is threatening key shipping lanes in the Red Sea and raising the risk of a broader regional war. It also directly impacts corporate earnings, as energy costs creep back up, threatening to derail the margin expansion we've seen in other sectors.

The City angle: For commodities desks and macro traders, $100+ Brent is a psychological and economic threshold. It complicates the Bank of England and Fed's plans for rate cuts, as energy-driven inflation could easily trigger a second wave of price hikes. It also benefits oil majors like BP and Shell, but acts as a heavy tax on the rest of the economy.

items: What to say at work: 'Brent touching $101 is a wake-up call that geopolitical risk premium is back with a vengeance. Even if it eases off, the threat of a wider conflict in Iran means energy volatility is going to keep central bankers on edge. It makes any near-term rate cut bets look increasingly risky.'

content.text: The Friday Wrap: Tech Wobbles, Tariffs Bite, and Patriot Missiles

If you spent Friday afternoon looking at your screens hoping for a quiet slide into the weekend, you were sorely disappointed. Friday capped off a bruising week for risk assets, particularly in tech land. The Nasdaq composite fell another 0.6% on Friday to close at 24,975.82, bringing its weekly loss to a painful 2.1%. The S&P 500 managed to scrape a flat finish, up a mere 0.05% to 7,411.98, while the price-weighted Dow Jones was the week's relative safe haven, rising 0.5% to 51,947.25. Underneath the surface, the cross-asset signals are flashing a very specific, stagflationary warning.
AI Capex Fatigue: Show Me the Money

The big story of the week was the $800 billion wipeout in Big Tech. We have officially entered the 'show me the money' phase of the AI cycle. It is not that corporate earnings are bad—FactSet notes that Q2 earnings growth is on track for its highest rate since 2021—but the market is losing its patience with the astronomical price tag. Alphabet’s earnings were technically a blowout, but the headline GAAP numbers were heavily distorted by a massive $98 billion paper gain on its SpaceX investment. Once you strip that out, investors stared directly at a massive, accelerating capital expenditure bill and blinked. When Tesla followed up with disappointing margins and heavy spending, the narrative solidified: hyperscalers are spending like drunken sailors, and the street is starting to question the return on investment timeline.
Intel’s Revenge

However, there was one massive, blue-tinted exception. Intel absolutely crushed its Q2 earnings, posting EPS of $0.42 (nearly double the $0.21 consensus) on revenue of $16.1 billion, up 25% year-on-year. It is Intel’s strongest revenue growth in over 15 years, driven by a 59% surge in Data Center & AI revenue. While the market is panicking about the hyperscalers' capex, Intel is proving that someone is actually pocketing that cash. With their 18A process node hitting key milestones, the turnaround thesis is finally gaining some real operational teeth.
The Geopolitical Stagflation Cocktail

Away from the trading desks, the macro backdrop is getting increasingly spicy. On Friday, the Trump administration’s new Section 301 'Forced Labor' tariffs officially took effect, slapping 10% to 12.5% duties on imports from 60 economies. This comes hot on the heels of a 50% tariff on Canadian goods under a dusted-off 1930s statute (Section 338). If you are building supply chain models, the era of frictionless trade is officially dead.

At the same time, the US-Iran war continues to strangle global logistics. Brent crude spiked to $102 a barrel on Thursday as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz slowed to a crawl, before easing back to $96.78 on Friday. The catalyst for the Friday pullback? A bizarrely pragmatic report that President Trump is pausing a major escalation because the US is literally running out of Patriot interceptor missiles, having fired over 1,200 during the conflict. It is a stark reminder of the physical limits of modern warfare—and modern supply chains.
The Cross-Asset Read: The Curve Disinverts (The Hard Way)

For the fixed income desks, the message is clear. The US 10-year Treasury yield closed the week at 4.69%, while the 2-year yield sat at 4.33%. Yes, the yield curve is no longer inverted—but this isn't the 'bull steepener' you were hoping for. Instead of short-term rates falling on the back of aggressive Fed cuts, the long end is surging. Bond vigilantes are pricing in a persistent, tariff-induced inflation impulse and a massive fiscal deficit to fund regional wars. If you are pitching an asset allocation strategy this week, the 'higher-for-longer' narrative isn't just back—it has got teeth.

sections.title: Financial Idea of the Day: The Public-Private Real Estate Disconnect

content.text: Implied vs. Appraisal Cap Rates

If you’ve spent any time looking at commercial real estate (CRE) recently, you’ll know the sector has been through the ringer. But if you look at the valuations reported by private property funds versus those priced in by the stock market for listed Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs), you’d think they were operating on different planets. This brings us to today’s crucial concept: the difference between the Appraisal Cap Rate and the Implied Cap Rate, and the massive valuation arbitrage it currently presents.
The Basics: What is a Cap Rate?

In real estate, the capitalisation rate (cap rate) is the fundamental pricing metric. It’s simply the property-level yield: Net Operating Income (NOI) divided by the property’s value. Think of it as the inverse of an EV/EBITDA multiple. A lower cap rate means investors are paying a higher multiple for every pound of rental income (typical for prime London offices or shiny logistics hubs). A higher cap rate means the asset is priced cheaply, reflecting higher risk or lower growth.
The Disconnect: Appraisal vs. Implied
The drama lies in how we determine "Property Value":

items: Appraisal Cap Rate (Private Market): Private funds value their portfolios using external appraisers. These appraisers look at historical transactions, make some spreadsheet assumptions, and declare what the properties are worth. The problem? Appraisers are notoriously slow, transactions have dried up, and nobody wants to be the first to write down their portfolio by 30%. This leads to "appraisal smoothing"—private valuations lag reality by quarters, if not years.

Implied Cap Rate (Public Market): Publicly traded REITs trade on the stock exchange every second. We can back out the property value the stock market is actually pricing in by looking at the REIT's Enterprise Value (EV). Because the stock market is liquid and forward-looking, it reprices instantly when interest rates jump.

content.text: A Simple Numerical Example
Imagine "Squire Estates", a REIT owning a portfolio of prime London logistics warehouses. The portfolio generates £100 million in Net Operating Income (NOI).

items: The Private View: The fund’s appraisers look at the high-quality tenants and say, "This portfolio is worth £2.0 billion." This gives us an Appraisal Cap Rate of 5.0% (£100m / £2.0bn).

The Public View: Meanwhile, Squire Estates is listed on the London Stock Exchange. Because interest rates have surged, investors have dumped the stock. Its market cap is now £600 million, and it has £800 million of net debt, giving it an implied real estate value (EV) of £1.4 billion.
The Implied Cap Rate: The stock market is pricing the exact same portfolio at £1.4 billion. This means the stock market is demanding an Implied Cap Rate of 7.14% (£100m / £1.4bn).
The Arbitrage: The public market is pricing the REIT at a whopping 30% discount to its Net Asset Value (NAV).

content.text: Why This Matters in Asset Management

Right now, we are living through one of the longest public-private real estate valuation dislocations in history. Public REIT implied cap rates have hovered significantly higher than private appraisal cap rates, which have remained stubbornly low—almost matching the 10-year Treasury yield, implying virtually zero risk premium for private real estate. This has massive real-world implications:

items: The Denominator Effect: Pension funds that set target allocations (e.g., 10% in real estate) find themselves "over-allocated" to private real estate simply because their private managers haven't written down their assets, while their public equity portfolios have fluctuated.

The Public-to-Private Arbitrage: Private equity giants like Blackstone have been raising massive pools of dry powder to buy public REITs at a discount, effectively buying high-quality real estate on the cheap compared to building it or buying it in the private market.
Capital Allocation: If you are an asset manager, buying private real estate at a 4.5% yield when you can buy the same assets via liquid public REITs at a 7% implied yield is a tough sell to clients.

content.text: Common Beginner Mistakes

items: Confusing Cap Rates with Returns: A cap rate is an unlevered, one-year cash yield. It doesn't account for leverage, capital expenditure (capex) required to keep the building standing, or future rent growth.

Mixing up the Direction: Remember, a lower cap rate means a higher valuation multiple. If cap rates "expand" (go up), property values are falling. If cap rates "compress" (go down), property values are rising.

Using Net Income instead of NOI: Beginners often use bottom-line Net Income to calculate cap rates. Don't. Net Income includes interest expense and corporate-level SG&A. Cap rates must be calculated using Net Operating Income (NOI) to keep it capital-structure neutral.

content.text: How to Use This in Interviews

If you are interviewing for a role in real estate private equity (REPE), asset management, or investment banking, this is a prime topic to show commercial sharpness. If asked: "How would you assess whether public REITs are cheap right now?"

You can answer: "I’d look at the spread between the REITs' implied cap rates and private market appraisal cap rates. Historically, public and private cap rates trade in tandem, but during rate-hiking cycles, public REITs reprice instantly, causing implied cap rates to expand. If implied cap rates are significantly higher than private appraisal cap rates—as they are now, with public REITs trading at a massive discount to NAV—it suggests the public market has already taken its medicine, while private markets are still suffering from appraisal smoothing. This represents a highly attractive entry point for public real estate."
Over a Pint: What to Say at the Pub

"Private real estate funds are basically living in a 2021 fantasy land. Their appraisers are marking to model, keeping cap rates artificially low and pretending there's no risk premium over the 10-year Treasury. Meanwhile, public REITs have faced reality, repriced, and are offering massive implied yields. If you're putting money to work in property today, you buy the public market at a 30% discount to NAV, or you sit on your hands until the private funds are forced to finally mark their portfolios to market."

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day: The Optimiser as an Implicit Prior

content.text: Same Loss, Different Portfolio

Imagine you’ve spent the last three weeks building a deep learning model to forecast daily volatility for S&P 500 stocks. You run your backtests, and you’re absolutely buzzing: your test-set Mean Squared Error (MSE) is identical to the decimal point across two different training runs. One was trained using standard Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), and the other using Adam. Since the predictive accuracy is identical, they must be the same model under the hood, right? Wrong. In fact, if you deploy them, one might trade three times as much as the other, eating all your alpha in transaction costs. Welcome to the world of underspecification.
The Concept: Underspecification & Optimiser Bias

In financial machine learning, we almost always operate in a low signal-to-noise ratio environment. When you train a highly flexible neural network on noisy financial time series, the model is 'underspecified'. This means there are many different parameter configurations (and thus many different mathematical functions) that can achieve the exact same out-of-sample test loss. They all 'tie' on the leaderboard, but they are not interchangeable.

But here is the catch: how you navigate the loss landscape determines which of these functions you actually land on. The optimiser you choose (SGD, Adam, RMSprop, etc.) acts as an implicit prior or inductive bias. It doesn't just find a minimum; it selects a specific type of minimum:

items: SGD is naturally attracted to flatter minima. In financial terms, this biases the model toward learning simpler, smoother, and more linear-like response profiles.
Adam and other adaptive or matrix-aware optimisers are happy to stably converge to sharper minima. This biases the model toward learning highly non-linear, complex, and sometimes 'jumpy' functions.

content.text: The Real-World Financial Impact

A March 2026 paper from MIT and other top institutions ('Same Error, Different Function: The Optimizer as an Implicit Prior in Financial Time Series') proved exactly how dangerous this is. The researchers trained 48 different model-pipeline combinations (including MLPs, CNNs, LSTMs, and Transformers) to forecast daily volatility on the S&P 500. Even when they strictly controlled hyperparameters so that all models achieved identical test RMSE, the actual functions learned were wildly different.

When they plugged these 'identical' forecasts into a standard volatility-ranked portfolio strategy, they found a near-vertical 'Sharpe-turnover frontier'. The Sharpe ratios of the portfolios were virtually identical (around 0.9), but the portfolio turnover varied by up to 3x! The Adam-trained models produced highly active, jumpy forecasts that triggered constant rebalancing, while the SGD-trained models produced smooth forecasts with low turnover. If you didn't account for transaction costs, you'd think they were the same. In production, the Adam model would bankrupt you on execution fees.
Mini Technical Example: Measuring Prediction Roughness

To avoid this trap, quant researchers must evaluate models beyond scalar loss. One simple diagnostic is to measure the 'roughness' or first-difference of the predictions, which serves as a proxy for implied portfolio turnover. Here is how you can implement this in PyTorch:

import torch

def evaluate_model_dynamics(model, X_test, y_test):
    """
    Evaluates both the standard predictive accuracy (MSE) 
    and the functional roughness (implied turnover proxy) of a model.
    """
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        predictions = model(X_test)  # Shape: (num_timesteps, num_assets)
        
        # 1. Standard Scalar Loss (MSE)
        mse = torch.mean((predictions - y_test) ** 2).item()
        
        # 2. Functional Roughness (First-difference volatility)
        # High roughness implies high portfolio turnover in production
        delta_preds = predictions[1:] - predictions[:-1]
        roughness = torch.mean(torch.abs(delta_preds)).item()
        
    return {
        "test_mse": mse,
        "implied_turnover_roughness": roughness
    }
The Pub / Interview Conversation Angle

This is a goldmine for interviews. If an interviewer asks you how you evaluate a machine learning model for trading, do not just say 'MSE' or 'out-of-sample R-squared'. That’s rookie level. Instead, drop this: 'In low signal-to-noise regimes like finance, models suffer from severe underspecification. Two models can have identical test MSE but learn completely different functions due to optimiser-induced inductive bias. I always evaluate the functional and decision-level metrics—like checking the first-difference roughness of the predictions or the Jacobian of the model—to ensure the optimiser isn't secretly pushing us into a high-turnover regime that gets eaten alive by transaction costs.'
Risks & Limitations

While SGD might give you smoother, lower-turnover predictions, it isn't a silver bullet. If the true underlying market regime undergoes a sudden, sharp structural break, a smoother model trained with SGD might be too slow to adapt, whereas a more responsive (albeit noisier) Adam-trained model might capture the regime shift faster. The key is to match your optimiser's implicit prior with your execution capabilities and the market environment.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading: The Demise of Short-Term Trend-Following

content.text: Alright, grab a pint. If you have spent any time around systematic CTAs or quant desks over the last decade, you will have heard the collective groaning about short-term trend-following. For nearly two centuries, buying what was going up and selling what was going down over short horizons (days to weeks) was a license to print money. Then, around 2009, the music stopped. Short-term momentum strategies flatlined, leaving quants scratching their heads and blaming everything from crowding to central bank intervention. But a brand-new working paper from the heavyweights at Capital Fund Management (CFM) and Imperial College London has cracked the case. And the answer is not what you think.
The Paper

The paper is titled 'Is Trend Still Your Friend?: A Microstructural Account of the Demise of Short-Term Trend-Following' (July 2026), co-authored by Jutta G. Kurth, Zoltan Eisler, Adam Rej, and the godfather of econophysics himself, Jean-Philippe Bouchaud.
Why This Matters

For years, the standard excuse for the death of short-term trend-following was crowding—too many quants chasing the same signals. But the authors point out a glaring flaw in this theory: CTA assets under management have actually stagnated since 2010, while overall market liquidity has grown. The footprint of trend followers has shrunk, yet the strategy still has not recovered. Market electronification also fails to explain the timing. Instead, the authors look under the hood of the limit order book (LOB) and find a beautifully elegant, microstructural explanation: volatility-normalised tick size.
The Core Discovery: Large-Tick vs. Small-Tick
The paper splits the futures universe into two camps based on their volatility-normalised tick size:

items: Large-tick contracts: Where the minimum price step (the tick) is large relative to daily volatility (e.g., short-term interest rate or bond futures, and some commodities). These order books are dense—there is always a massive queue of orders waiting at each price level.

Small-tick contracts: Where the tick size is a tiny fraction of daily volatility (e.g., currency futures, equity indices). These books are sparse—orders are scattered thinly across many different price levels.

content.text: The empirical finding is stark: post-2008, trend-following P&L completely collapsed on small-tick contracts across all signal horizons. Meanwhile, on large-tick contracts, trend-following remains as profitable and robust as it ever was. Neither asset class nor overall liquidity explains this split—it is purely a function of the tick size.
The HFT Liquidity Trap

Why does tick size dictate strategy survival? It comes down to a self-fulfilling feedback loop. Trend-following works because when quants get a buy signal, they place aggressive market orders. This buying pressure has a physical market impact, pushing the price up and reinforcing the very trend that triggered the signal. Market impact is the actual engine of momentum. But post-2008, market making was taken over by high-frequency trading (HFT) algorithms. HFTs are terrified of toxic (predictable, directional) order flow. When they detect a trend-follower buying, they immediately pull their liquidity to avoid getting run over.

In a sparse, small-tick book, this liquidity withdrawal is catastrophic. The bid-ask spread widens instantly, and the trend-follower suffers massive slippage. This execution cost eats up all the alpha, breaking the self-fulfilling loop. In a dense, large-tick book, however, the massive queue of passive orders acts as a buffer. Even when HFTs pull back, there is still enough residual depth to absorb the trend-follower's trades without ruinous slippage. The loop survives, and the trend continues to deliver.
Key Takeaways

items: Market impact is the engine, not just a cost: Momentum is not just a passive anomaly; it is actively sustained by the market impact of the trend followers themselves.
Microstructure dictates macro returns: A simple exchange rule—the tick size—can completely destroy or preserve a multi-billion-dollar investment strategy.

Where to find alpha: If you are building momentum models, stop wasting time on small-tick contracts (like FX or equity indices) and focus your short-term signals where the queues are thick (large-tick bond and rate futures).

content.text: What to Skim vs. What to Read

Skim Section 5 and the appendices if you do not want to drown in the heavy mathematical derivations of price-impact models and limit order book dynamics. Instead, focus on the empirical charts in Section 3 and 4, which show the incredibly clean divergence in cumulative P&L between the small-tick and large-tick portfolios.
Over a Pint: What to Say at Work

Have you seen the new CFM paper on why short-term trend following died? It is not about crowding or CTA assets growing too big. It is actually a microstructural story about volatility-normalised tick size. HFTs withdraw liquidity in sparse, small-tick books when they see directional flow, which blows up slippage and breaks the self-fulfilling price impact loop. But in dense, large-tick books like bond futures, the trend loop is still alive and kicking.
Our Take

This is a masterclass in quantitative research. It bridges the gap between high-frequency microstructure and medium-frequency asset pricing, showing that market design has profound, unintended consequences on macro investment strategies. It is a reminder that in modern markets, you cannot design a successful trading strategy without deeply understanding the plumbing of the exchanges you trade on.

sections.title: People / Business Psychology Idea: The Security Blanket Bias

content.text: Why More Data Often Leads to Worse Decisions

We've all been there. It's Thursday night, the investment committee is at 9:00 AM tomorrow, and the VP is sweating over their third double-espresso. "We need more data on the target's logistics footprint in East Anglia," they bark. You spend all night pulling together a 20-page appendix on some obscure regulatory tweak. Come Friday, the committee doesn't even look at it because the deal is entirely a play on the target's IP. You, my friend, have just fallen victim to Information Bias.

First formalised by psychologists Jonathan Baron, Jane Beattie, and John C. Hershey in 1988, Information Bias is our psychological tendency to seek out extra information even when it cannot possibly affect our actions or decisions. We treat data like a security blanket. We crave it because it reduces our immediate anxiety, confusing "having more information" with "making a better decision". In reality, we often end up with the exact same decision, just twelve hours later, £50k poorer, and severely sleep-deprived.
The Diagnostic Trap

In their classic experiment, the researchers presented participants with a medical diagnosis problem. A patient had symptoms that pointed to a specific disease with an 80% probability. The participants were offered the chance to run a diagnostic test. Crucially, even if the test came back positive or negative, the recommended treatment would remain exactly the same.

Logically, the test was useless. It had zero diagnostic value for the actual decision. Yet, the vast majority of participants insisted on running the test anyway. Why? Because they wanted "certainty". They wanted to feel like they were doing something, rather than sitting with the discomfort of a probabilistic bet.
How This Plays Out in the City

In the City, this manifests as "analysis paralysis" masquerading as "rigorous due diligence." It's the portfolio manager who refuses to pull the trigger on a macro trade until they've read a 100-page broker report on a minor sub-segment that represents 0.5% of the index. It's the M&A team commissioning a bespoke market study on a division the buyer plans to immediately spin off anyway.
This isn't just harmless over-preparation. It carries massive hidden costs:

items: Opportunity Cost: While you are waiting for the "perfect" data set, the market moves, the competitor bids, or the window of opportunity slams shut.
Cognitive Fatigue: Sifting through irrelevant data dilutes your focus. You lose the forest for the trees, focusing on minor details rather than the core drivers of the asset's value.
False Confidence: Having more data makes us feel more confident, but not necessarily more accurate. You end up over-leveraged on a bad trade because you have a "really thorough" model.

content.text: How to Use This at Work
The next time a senior stakeholder asks for "one more cut of the data" or "some extra colour on X," don't just blindly open Excel. Run the "So What?" Test.
Ask yourself (and, if you have the political capital, your boss):

items: "If this data comes back showing X, what is our decision?"
"If this data comes back showing Y, what is our decision?"

content.text: If the answer to both questions is identical, the data is noise. You don't need it.

If you are managing upwards, you can frame it constructively: "We can absolutely pull that data, but given our core thesis is driven by [Factor A], even a negative result on [Factor B] wouldn't change our recommendation to buy. To save time and keep us moving fast, should we focus on finalising the valuation instead?" It makes you look commercially sharp, highly efficient, and focused on what actually moves the needle.
One Line to Remember
If the answer won't change your move, stop looking for the answer.
